definition: The all-in yearly cost of owning and running an accelerator (capital charge on the hardware, network, facility, power and operations) divided by its hours. It is what a GPU-hour costs the owner, as opposed to the rental price a customer pays.

Owner cost of an accelerator over a period divided by the tokens it produced, scaled to one million. It depends as much on throughput at a chosen speed per user and on utilization as on the hardware price.

The annual return investors require on the money tied up in an asset (weighted average cost of capital). In a TCO model it turns upfront capex into a level yearly charge that includes financing, not just depreciation.

How long hardware keeps earning more than its cash running costs. It can be shorter than the accounting useful life when newer chips make tokens much cheaper, which is the core of the GPU-depreciation bear case.
Spreading an asset's cost evenly over its useful life (for example a $70K GPU over six years = ~$11.7K a year). It ignores financing cost, which a capital recovery factor adds.
What an asset can be sold for at the end of its use. Positive resale prices for old GPUs lower their true cost; falling rental prices lower residual values and can force impairments.
The share of installed accelerator-hours that do paid or useful work. Because most of an accelerator's cost is fixed, cost per useful hour scales with 1 ÷ utilization.
The average share of full power a facility actually draws. Idle accelerators still draw some power, so a TCO model charges a floor plus the busy share.

Spending on the building, electrical plant, cooling and land around the IT equipment, usually quoted per MW of power (roughly $11-13M per MW for new AI halls in this repo's estimates). It lasts longer than the servers inside.

The speed per user (tokens per second per user) at which a system is run. Throughput and cost per token change sharply along the throughput-interactivity frontier, so any cost comparison must name its operating point.

A model feature, used by DeepSeek, that drafts several future tokens per step so the server can verify them together: a built-in form of speculative decoding that can raise throughput several-fold at the same speed per user.
A sensitivity chart that changes one input at a time between a low and a high value and sorts the inputs by how far they move the result, so the widest bars show which assumptions matter most.
Re-running a model thousands of times with inputs drawn at random from their plausible ranges, then reporting percentiles (e.g. P10-P90) of the output instead of a single number.

A thought experiment: if a rival's accelerator system cost nothing, would its cost per token still be higher than NVIDIA's at full price? It holds only where the throughput gap is larger than the share of cost that is chip capex.
Calendar days a training run takes on a given cluster. Faster chips or larger clusters shorten it; for a frontier lab, earlier model release can be worth more than the compute bill.

The hourly price at which renting an older accelerator yields the same cost per token as the newest generation. When new chips cut cost per token, the parity rent of old ones falls, dragging rental prices down.
